# Contributing to OpenMRS

## Resources for Getting Started

Your contributions are what make OpenMRS an awesome Health IT system in developing countries. We want to make it as easy and fun as possible for you to contribute to the project and interact with the community. Before you get started contributing to OpenMRS, we encourage you to read both our [OpenMRS Developers Guide](http://om.rs/newdev) and our [Getting Started as a Developer](https://wiki.openmrs.org/x/MQAJ) wiki page.

## Reporting Bugs

1. Please check to see if you are running the latest version of OpenMRS; the bug may already be resolved. If you are running an old version, it may no longer be supported. Check our [Unsupported Releases](https://wiki.openmrs.org/x/2RAz) page for details.

2. Search for similar problems using the [OpenMRS Global Search](http://search.openmrs.org); it may already be an identified problem.

3. Make sure you can reproduce your problem on our demo site at [demo.openmrs.org](http://demo.openmrs.org).

4. If you know the problem is related to the function or performance of a specific add-on module you're running, please consult the [Module Repository](http://modules.openmrs.org) and that module's documentation about how to get support.

5. If you believe the problem is with OpenMRS itself, or if you're honestly not sure, you can [file the bug report in the OpenMRS Trunk project in JIRA](https://tickets.openmrs.org/secure/CreateIssue.jspa?pid=10000&issuetype=1&Create=Create). You'll need to have an [OpenMRS ID](http://id.openmrs.org) to do so. You'll receive e-mail updates as the bug is investigated and resolved.

### Bug report contents

Regardless of whether you're reporting the bug to the OpenMRS core team or to a module developer, to help those developers understand the problem, please include as much information as possible:

1. A clear description of how to recreate the error, including any error messages shown.
2. The version of OpenMRS you are using.
3. The type and version of the database you are using, if known.
4. If you are using any additional modules, custom templates, stylesheets, or messages, please list them.
5. If applicable, please copy and paste the full Java stack trace.
6. If you have already communicated with a developer about this issue, please provide their name.

rows.title: Stop the JVM aborting the openmrs-api test fork on Java 8 and 11
rows.excerpt:
## Description of what I changed

Since 24 July the `openmrs-api` surefire fork has been aborting part way through the suite on 2.8.x, which fails nearly every pull request against the branch (#6394, #6262, #6230, #6219, and the last two pushes to 2.8.x itself). Every test that ran passed, so the build reported `Process Exit Code: 134` with no test failures to point at, and contributors have been pushing empty "re-run CI" commits to get around it.

#6399 makes CI keep the JVM's own crash log, and with that the Java 11 failure is no longer a mystery:

```
#  Internal Error (moduleEntry.cpp:263), pid=2394, tid=2395
#  guarantee(java_lang_Module::is_instance(module)) failed: The unnamed module for ClassLoader
#  jdk.internal.reflect.DelegatingClassLoader, is null or not an instance of java.lang.Module.
#  The class loader has not been initialized correctly.
# JRE version: OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-11.0.31+11
```

reached like this:

```
V  [libjvm.so+0xc1828a]  ModuleEntry::create_unnamed_module(ClassLoaderData*)+0xca
V  [libjvm.so+0x61eb86]  ClassLoaderDataGraph::add(Handle, bool)+0x216
V  [libjvm.so+0xf139db]  Unsafe_DefineClass0+0x37b
J  jdk.internal.reflect.MethodAccessorGenerator.generate(...)
J  jdk.internal.reflect.NativeConstructorAccessorImpl.newInstance(...)
J  org.mockito.internal.util.reflection.ReflectionMemberAccessor$$Lambda$1524.newInstance()
j  org.mockito.internal.creation.bytebuddy.InlineDelegateByteBuddyMockMaker.lambda$newInstance$4(...)
```

The crash needs the JDK to **inflate a reflective accessor**. Once a reflective member has been invoked more than `sun.reflect.inflationThreshold` times (15 by default), the JDK stops using the native accessor, generates a bytecode accessor, and defines it into a `jdk.internal.reflect.DelegatingClassLoader` — and creating that loader's unnamed module is what trips the guarantee. Mockito's inline mock maker reaches that path while instantiating a mock, so a suite creating thousands of mocks in one fork gets there reliably.

Raising the threshold out of reach keeps reflection on the native accessor for the whole run, so no accessor is ever generated and the crashing path is never entered.

I checked that rather than assuming it. On Temurin 11 with `-verbose:class`, reflectively invoking a constructor 200 times:

rows.excerpt:
<!--- Add a pull request title above in this format -->
<!--- real example: 'TRUNK-5111: Replace use of deprecated isVoided' -->
<!--- 'TRUNK-JiraIssueNumber: JiraIssueTitle' -->
## Description of what I changed
<!--- Describe your changes in detail -->
<!--- It can simply be your commit message, which you must have -->
OpenMRS now speaks OpenTelemetry!

openmrs-core can now export OpenTelemetry metrics. bundles the OTel Java agent and attaches it when `OMRS_OTEL_ENABLED`=true.

off by default. nothing changes for anyone who doesn't opt in.

### Why do we need this?

Implementers currently have no standard way to see whether an openmrs server is healthy. everyone builds their own thing, in whatever shape, so nothing's shareable.

OTel is a CNCF standard that basically every observability backend speaks. So instead of us picking a monitoring vendor for people, we emit a standard format and they point it wherever:

_"openmrs exports standard OTel. Grab it however you like."_

**Why core and not the distro:** bahmni, kenyaEMR, ugandaEMR and the rest all build on core. distro-only means each of them reimplements it. also the attach logic has to live in startup.sh anyway, and that's here.

**Why the java agent and not a JMX scraper**: runs in-process, exposes nothing. a scraper needs every deployment to open a JMX/RMI port, which is a rough default for a clinical system.

### What changed

Dockerfile: downloads the agent to /openmrs/otel in the production stage, checksum-verified, same pattern as the tini and tomcat downloads. Pure java so no TARGETARCH handling needed.

startup.sh: appends -javaagent: to CATALINA_OPTS when the flag is set. mirrors the existing OMRS_DEV_DEBUG_PORT block right above it. uses ${VAR-} since the script runs under -u.

that's it. everything past the on/off flag is standard `OTEL_*` variables, so the config surface is the OTel spec rather than something we invented.

Sample config:
```
        OMRS_OTEL_ENABLED: true
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://alloy:4317
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL: grpc
        OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: openmrs-backend
        OTEL_JMX_TARGET_SYSTEM: tomcat
        OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER: otlp
        OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER: none
        OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER: none
```

rows.title: TRUNK-6708: Map uuid as a Hibernate natural id and serve by-uuid lookups from cache
rows.excerpt:
## Description of what I changed

Looking an entity up by uuid ran a criteria query on the uuid column, so every `get*ByUuid` call went to the database, even when the entity was already in the second-level cache. This maps `uuid` as an immutable Hibernate natural id and routes the shared by-uuid lookup through the natural id API, so cached entities are returned without a database round trip.

- `@NaturalId` on `BaseOpenmrsObject.uuid` covers the annotated entities. The hbm.xml mappings wrap their uuid property in `<natural-id>`.
- Entities that are already cached also cache their natural ids, with `@NaturalIdCache` next to `@Cache`, or `<natural-id-cache>` in hbm.xml. The hbm.xml binder has no default region for natural ids (a bare `<natural-id-cache/>` silently caches nothing), so those mappings name the region the annotation would use, `org.openmrs.<Entity>##NaturalId`.
- `HibernateUtil.getUniqueEntityByUUID` loads with `session.find(entityClass, uuid, KeyType.NATURAL)` when uuid is the only natural id of the entity. It keeps the existing query for a null uuid, for entities without that natural id (for example, module entities mapped without one), and when a filter enabled on the session restricts the entity. Loading by natural id does not apply Hibernate filters, not even on a cache hit, so without that last check, filters like the ones the Data Filter module defines would stop hiding records looked up by uuid. With no filter enabled, the check returns right away.
- `Context.evictAllEntities(Class)` also evicts the natural id cache of the class.
- `HibernateOrderDAO.deleteObsThatReference`: the bulk delete bypasses the session, and a natural id lookup checks the session first, so the deleted obs are now detached. Otherwise `getObsByUuid` could return an obs that was just deleted (caught by `OrderServiceTest.purgeOrder_shouldDeleteAnyObsAssociatedToTheOrderWhenCascadeIsTrue`).
- The `OpenmrsObject.setUuid` javadoc now says the uuid is the natural id and cannot change once the object is saved, so an externally determined uuid has to be set before the first save.

Behavior change: Hibernate now rejects a change to the uuid of an object that is already saved. Before, hbm.xml entities allowed it and annotated entities silently ignored it. No code in core changes a saved uuid (I went through every `setUuid` call), but two concept conversion tests did, by saving

rows.title: TRUNK-6823: Deny with APIAuthenticationException again, as an AuthorizationDeniedException
rows.excerpt:
## Description of what I changed

Since TRUNK-6799, `AuthorizationAdvice` and core's explicit privilege checks deny with Spring Security's `AccessDeniedException` instead of `APIAuthenticationException`. Code that catches the old type no longer sees these denials. webservices.rest maps only that type, so REST now answers 500 where it answered 401 or 403.

This keeps `AccessDeniedException` as the type a denial is. It only makes the deprecated exception a subtype of it:

- `APIAuthenticationException` now extends `AuthorizationDeniedException`. Its constructors keep their messages and causes, and it gains one that takes an `AuthorizationResult`. It stays `@Deprecated`, pointing new code at `AccessDeniedException`.
- `@Authorized` denies with it again (`AuthorizationAdvice`'s three throw sites), and so do the checks #6544 had switched to `AccessDeniedException`: `Daemon.runInNewDaemonThread`/`runNewDaemonTask`, `UserContext.becomeUser`, `AlertServiceImpl.getAlerts` and `TestInstallUtil.getResourceInputStream`.
- `PrivilegeNamingAuthorizationManager` returns it as the result when a `@PreAuthorize`/`@PostAuthorize` check names the missing privilege, and when `isAuthenticated()` denies a caller who is not logged in. The second case carries "Basic authentication required", as `@Authorized()` does. Spring's default handler throws that result, so converting a method by the guide's translation table keeps what its callers catch. Only an expression that names neither, such as `denyAll()`, still denies with a plain `AuthorizationDeniedException`. URL rules are unchanged.
- `doc/AUTHORIZATION_MIGRATION.md`, `ExceptionUtil` and the exception's javadoc say so. The guide has a Pitfalls row for the `VerifyError` below.

webservices.rest still needs RESTWS-1056 (openmrs/openmrs-module-webservices.rest#767) for denials that are not an `APIAuthenticationException`.

**Compatibility.** `APIAuthenticationException` is no longer an `APIException`.

- **Compiled bytecode that treats it as one fails JVM verification.** A module built against an earlier core breaks until it is rebuilt.
- **Example: patientdocuments.** It has `catch (APIAuthenticationException | ContextAuthenticationException e)` in two controllers, which javac types as `APIException`.
